Some Notes on Nomenclature – Experimentation Depending on the context, there are different definitions of what constitutes an experiment.  Since the point of this talk is to attempt to broaden the scope and responsibilities of an experimentation team, I am using the more general sense of the term. The purpose of any experiment is to learn something.  We might be trying to establish causality or prove an outcome, or understand what users find confusing, or see if we understand a compliance constraint, or we simply might want to learn why our ideas are not working as well as we hoped.  We might be trying to prove something, or we might simply be trying to better understand why the results are what they are.  There are of course very different techniques used for each, and very different levels of data rigor, depending on the objective of the experiment. More generally, many of our experiments are precisely because we want to avoid building and testing the wrong thing. – Product Model This talk focuses on experimentation in the product operating model .  Yet most companies use the old project model , where stakeholders create product roadmaps of projects and features, and assign those to product teams to build and launch (output).  In contrast, in the product model, product teams are instead given problems to solve, and they are then empowered to come up with a solution that delivers the necessary business results (outcomes). Experimentation still happens in the project model, but it’s mostly optimization work.  But if your goal is innovation and achieving outcomes, then this is where the broader role of experimentation becomes an essential competency. Overview The product operating model is all about consistent innovation as the key to delivering outcomes, and experimentation is at the very core of the product model.  As Jeff Bezos explains, “If you want to innovate, you simply must experiment.”   While AI is already impacting the mechanics and tasks involved with planning, running and evaluating many types of experiments, the larger role of experimentation, and what we call “building to learn,” has never been more important.  In this talk, we’ll describe what we see as the necessary future of this broader and deeper role of experimentation. Introduction I don’t remember precisely when I did my first qualitative product discovery experiment.  It would have been in the early 1980’s, and it would have involved creating and testing a prototype with a set of customers. I do remember when I did my first quantitative product discovery experiment.  In 1997 I was running a product organization at Netscape Communications, during the early rapid growth of the Internet.  I was dealing with the (still common) problem of an executive that had a very strong opinion about a product’s design, yet I had a product designer with a very different opinion. I mentioned this issue to our company’s design leader, Hugh Dubberly, who had joined us after being a design leader at Apple. Hugh explained that since the service we were running had a high volume of traffic (we were one of the first companies that had literally millions of daily active users), we could use data to run an A/B test and determine which treatment performed better. Our CEO was Jim Barksdale, and one of the principles he drilled into us was: “If we have data, let’s look at data. If all we have are opinions, let’s go with mine.”   It was the Internet that enabled product teams to collect the necessary volume of data that made data-informed decisions viable. It’s hard to describe just how empowering that was; to be able to have the tools to pursue ideas, and overcome the objections of more senior leaders. Moreover, the product model is all about delivering outcomes, and the way we attribute is with live-data experiments. The Internet opened up a world of new possibilities, but today, AI has gone further to both change the calculus of product development (where we spend our time), and to change the nature of many of the products we are building (from deterministic to probabilistic). The time and cost of building has dropped dramatically, which means companies can ship more capabilities than ever before. And for the past year, that is very much what has happened. Initially companies thought they could simply build quickly, release into the wild, and see what sticks, but the high failure rates come with serious consequences such as frustrated and confused customers, loss of customer trust, and high churn.  Even more importantly, few have seen a corresponding improvement to the outcomes .
